summary: Describes a TFTP option that lets the client and server negotiate a block size better matched to the network medium, instead of using the default small blocks. It is a draft standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of always sending a file in tiny pieces, the computers agree on a bigger piece size that fits the road.

questions: how to speed up tftp transfers
what is the tftp blocksize option
what is the maximum tftp block size
subtitle: Lets a TFTP client and server agree on a bigger block size than the default 512 octets.

tldr.problem: TFTP sends files in 512-octet blocks, which is not efficient on a LAN whose MTU may be 1500 octets or greater.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a blksize option to its read or write request. The server answers with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK) carrying a block size no larger than the one requested.
tldr.outcome: Larger blocks mean fewer packets and fewer acknowledgements. In the RFC's tests on a lightly loaded Ethernet, an 8192-octet block size cut transfer time by 80% compared with 512 octets.

today: RFC 2348 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1783 and updates RFC 1350. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Bigger Blocks
sections.content:
RFC 1350 defines TFTP, a simple, lock-step file transfer protocol. One of its main uses is booting diskless nodes on a local area network, and it is popular because it is small enough to fit in a tiny node's ROM space.

The catch is the fixed 512-octet block size. That is not the most efficient choice on a LAN whose MTU may be 1500 octets or greater. This RFC adds a TFTP option, built on the option extension mechanism of RFC 2347, so the client and server can negotiate a block size that suits the network medium.
sections.eli5: Sending a big file in tiny envelopes takes a lot of trips. This note lets both sides agree to use bigger envelopes.

sections.title: The Blocksize Option
sections.content:
The read request or write request packet gets two extra NULL-terminated fields after the mode: the option name blksize (case-insensitive) and the number of octets, written in ASCII. Valid values run from 8 to 65464 octets, inclusive. The block size counts data octets only, not the four octets of TFTP header.

The RFC's example is a read request (opcode 1) for the file foobar in octet mode with a block size of 1428, which is the Ethernet MTU less the TFTP, UDP and IP header lengths.
sections.eli5: You write a note on the request: "please use pieces this big." The number can be small or very large, but not outside the allowed range.

sections.title: Negotiating and Finishing
sections.content:
If the server accepts the option, it sends an Option Acknowledgment (OACK). The value in the OACK must be less than or equal to the value the client asked for. The client must then either use the size in the OACK or send an ERROR packet with error code 8 to end the transfer.

The rule for the final packet is unchanged from RFC 1350: a data packet shorter than the negotiated block size is the last one. If the file is smaller than the block size, the first packet is the last. If the file is an exact multiple of the block size, an extra data packet with no data ends the transfer.
sections.eli5: You ask for big pieces and the other side can say "that big or smaller." You either accept or walk away. The last piece is always the one that is not full.

sections.title: Measured Speedup and Security
sections.content:
The authors tested a prototype between two HP-UX 9000 machines in octet mode, using 2.25MB files on a lightly loaded Ethernet. Without a gateway, going from 512 to 8192 octets cut the transfer time by 80%. The gain comes mainly from sending fewer packets: doubling the block size halves both the data packets and the acknowledgements, and the sender waits for an ACK half as often. A smaller effect is less per-packet framing and processing overhead.

If the block size exceeds the path MTU, IP fragmentation and reassembly add overhead, and this is more noticeable the more gateways are on the path. On security, TFTP has none and this document adds none, but the RFC says the extensions add no additional security risks.
sections.eli5: Fewer, bigger boxes means less waiting for "got it!" messages. But if a box is too big for the road, it has to be cut up and glued back, which slows things down.
